Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Here $N$ is the supplied smooth timelike field selecting the future cone, and $o$ is an independent orientation. Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free, $g$-compatible connection of [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Use the curvature sign and contractions of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]; in particular $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 Sg_{ab}$. The geometric and observer conventions are those of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. The tangent-bundle smooth structure inherits only the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from [[def-countable-choice]].

Fix formal parameters $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $G_N>0$ and $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$. In length coordinates $x^0=ct$, all four coordinates have units metres and $g_{ab}$ is dimensionless. These are mathematical parameters with the displayed SI bookkeeping; they assert no measured value, exactness of $\mu_0$, or physical law.

A field strength $F$ is a real $C^2$ antisymmetric covariant two-tensor field. Its metric-raised components are $F^{ab}=g^{ac}g^{bd}F_{cd}$. For a future unit observer $n$ ($g(n,n)=-1$), the rest space is $n^\perp$ and the projection is $h_n(v)=v+g(n,v)n$. The observer electric and magnetic covectors are $E_{n,a}=cF_{ab}n^b$ and $B_{n,a}=-({\star_gF})_{ab}n^b$, with the oriented Lorentzian Hodge convention of [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]]. They annihilate $n$ and use the positive metric induced on the rest covector space. In a positively oriented orthonormal tetrad with time vector $n$, $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$.

For such an $F$, define

$$T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{ab}:=\frac1{\mu_0}\left(F^{ac}F^b{}_c-\frac14g^{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd}\right),\qquad T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}:=g_{ac}g_{bd}T_{\mathrm{EM}}^{cd}.$$

For any symmetric covariant tensor $S_{ab}$ and unit observer $n$, its observer energy density is $S_{ab}n^an^b$. Its observer energy-current vector is $-S^a{}_bn^b$; the spatial energy flux measured by $n$ is the projection $h_n(-S^a{}_bn^b)$ into $n^\perp$. A nonzero causal vector is future-directed when it has negative inner product with $N$; future timelike means $g(v,v)<0$, and future null means the vector is nonzero and $g(v,v)=0$.

In four dimensions, define the **weak energy condition** (WEC) for $S$ by $S_{ab}v^av^b\ge0$ for every future timelike $v$; the **null energy condition** (NEC) by $S_{ab}\ell^a\ell^b\ge0$ for every nonzero future null $\ell$; and the **dominant energy condition** (DEC) by requiring $-S^a{}_bv^b$ to be future causal or zero for every future timelike $v$. Define the **strong energy condition** (SEC) by the WEC for $S_{ab}-\tfrac12(g^{cd}S_{cd})g_{ab}$. These are definitions of tensor inequalities only; no general matter positivity premise is included.

A matter tensor $T_m^{ab}$ is a $C^1$ symmetric contravariant two-tensor field; a current $j^a$ is a $C^1$ vector field. The **formal sourced Maxwell equations** are $dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$. The **matter exchange equation** is $\nabla_aT_m^{ab}=F^b{}_cj^c$. The **formal Einstein equation** is

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa\bigl(T_{m,ab}+T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}\bigr).$$

Here $T_{m,ab}$ is obtained by lowering both indices with $g$. Each displayed equation is a pointwise mathematical condition on the supplied fields with the regularities stated above. A formal Einstein–Maxwell–matter solution is a tuple satisfying whichever of these equations are explicitly assumed on the stated open domain; no existence or uniqueness of such a tuple is asserted.

Two matter forms used below are defined as follows. A **charged-dust form** has $T_m^{ab}=\rho U^aU^b$ and $j^a=\sigma U^a$, where $\rho,\sigma\in C^1$, $\rho\ge0$, and $U\in C^2$ is future timelike with $g(U,U)=-c^2$. On $\{\rho>0\}$ its charge-to-mass ratio is $\alpha=\sigma/\rho$; it is not defined by division on $\{\rho=0\}$. A **perfect-fluid form** has

$$T_m^{ab}=\frac{\epsilon+p}{c^2}U^aU^b+pg^{ab},$$

where $\epsilon,p\in C^1$ and $U$ has the same timelike normalization. No equation of state, conductivity law, entropy law, or matter evolution theorem is part of this definition. A current may additionally be written $j^a=\sigma U^a+q^a$ with $q^aU_a=0$; an Ohmic relation $q^a=\chi E_U^a$, $\chi\ge0$, is a separately imposed constitutive hypothesis, where $E_U^a=F^a{}_bU^b$.

On an open set $V$, a **local potential** for $F$ is a supplied smooth one-form $A$ with $dA=F$. Such a potential need not exist globally. A local gauge change is $A\mapsto A+d\lambda$ for a supplied smooth scalar $\lambda$; this leaves $F$ unchanged. No global bundle, potential, or point-source construction is asserted.

In the stated length-coordinate SI interpretation, $[F_{ab}]=\mathrm T$, $[A_a]=\mathrm{T\,m}$, $[j^a]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $[T_m]=[T_{\mathrm{EM}}]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\sigma]=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, $[\alpha]=\mathrm{C\,kg^{-1}}$, $[\epsilon]=[p]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $[\chi]=\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}$. The equalities $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$ make the displayed tensor equations dimensionally consistent. No distributional product or stress tensor for a singular point source is defined.

Use the mathematical Lorentzian and SI conventions of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Fix a length scale $L>0$, a speed $c>0$, a nonzero constant charge-to-mass parameter $\alpha=q/m$, and choose $0<\epsilon\le\epsilon_*\le1$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\mathcal K\Subset\Omega$ be a compact convex set. Use length coordinates $x^0=ct$ and $x^i=LX^i$, with $X\in\Omega$ dimensionless. Assume a smooth stationary (independent of $x^0$) Lorentzian metric $g^{(\epsilon)}$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on a neighborhood of $\mathbb R_{x^0}\times L\mathcal K$, with $\partial_0$ chosen future timelike and $t$ increasing along the considered curves, whose components have the form

$$ g_{00}^{(\epsilon)}(X)=-(1+2\epsilon\phi(X))+r_{00}^{(\epsilon)}(X),\qquad g_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}(X)=(1-2\epsilon\phi(X))\delta_{ij}+r_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}(X),\qquad g_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}(X)=r_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}(X). $$

Here $\phi$ is dimensionless and smooth. A spatial multi-index is $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, with $|\beta|=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3$ and $\partial_X^\beta:=\partial_{X^1}^{\beta_1}\partial_{X^2}^{\beta_2}\partial_{X^3}^{\beta_3}$. For each such $\beta$ with $|\beta|\le2$, assume the uniform bounds

$$ |\partial_X^\beta r_{00}^{(\epsilon)}|+ \max_{i,j}|\partial_X^\beta r_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}| \le C_g\epsilon^2,\qquad \max_i|\partial_X^\beta r_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}|\le C_g\epsilon^{3/2} $$

on $\mathcal K$, with a fixed finite nonnegative $C_g$. Let $\mathbf e,\mathbf b:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth dimensionless fields whose values and first derivatives are bounded on $\mathcal K$. Since $\mathcal K$ is compact, the fixed smooth function $\phi$ and its derivatives used below are also bounded there. Prescribe a smooth stationary (independent of $x^0$) real two-form $F^{(\epsilon)}$ by its Cartesian components

$$ F_{0i}^{(\epsilon)}=-E_i^{(\epsilon)}/c,\qquad F_{ij}^{(\epsilon)}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k^{(\epsilon)},\qquad \alpha\mathbf E^{(\epsilon)}(X)=\frac{\epsilon c^2}{L}\mathbf e(X),\qquad \alpha\mathbf B^{(\epsilon)}(X)=\frac{\sqrt\epsilon\,c}{L}\mathbf b(X). $$

No Maxwell or Einstein equation for this prescribed background field or metric is assumed. Define the dimensionless potential $\phi$ comparison system on $S\in[0,S_*]$ by

$$ \frac{d\mathbf X_N}{dS}=\mathbf W_N,\qquad \frac{d\mathbf W_N}{dS}=-\nabla_X\phi(\mathbf X_N)+\mathbf e(\mathbf X_N)+\mathbf W_N\times\mathbf b(\mathbf X_N), $$

where $(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)_i:=\sum_{j,k}\epsilon_{ijk}u_jv_k$. Let $f(\mathbf X,\mathbf W)$ denote the six-component right-hand side of this system. Assume that on a compact convex state set $\mathcal Q\subseteq\mathcal K\times\mathbb R^3$, containing both trajectories, its derivative satisfies $\|Df\|_{1\to1}\le L_f$ for a finite nonnegative $L_f$. Here $\|(\mathbf X,\mathbf W)\|_1$ is the sum of the absolute values of its six real components, and $\|Df\|_{1\to1}$ is the operator norm induced by this $\ell^1$ norm.

For each $\epsilon$, let $z_\epsilon$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve, parameterized by proper time $\tau$ as in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], that solves the prescribed external Lorentz equation

$$ \nabla_U U=\alpha F^{(\epsilon)\sharp}(U),\qquad g^{(\epsilon)}(U,U)=-c^2,\qquad U=\frac{dz_\epsilon}{d\tau}. $$

Write its coordinate velocity as $\mathbf w=d\mathbf x/dt$ and assume $|\mathbf w|\le C_v\sqrt\epsilon\,c$ on $[0,S_*]$ for a fixed finite $C_v$. Suppose the relativistic scaled trajectory $(\mathbf X_\epsilon,\mathbf W_\epsilon)$ and the comparison trajectory $(\mathbf X_N,\mathbf W_N)$ exist throughout $[0,S_*]$, remain in $\mathcal Q$, and have the same initial data, where

$$ \mathbf X:=\mathbf x/L,\qquad \mathbf W:=\mathbf w/(\sqrt\epsilon\,c),\qquad S:=\sqrt\epsilon\,ct/L. $$

Then, after choosing $\epsilon_*>0$ sufficiently small in terms of the stated uniform constants, the exact relativistic trajectory satisfies

$$ \frac{d\mathbf X_\epsilon}{dS}=\mathbf W_\epsilon,\qquad \frac{d\mathbf W_\epsilon}{dS} =-\nabla_X\phi(\mathbf X_\epsilon)+\mathbf e(\mathbf X_\epsilon) +\mathbf W_\epsilon\times\mathbf b(\mathbf X_\epsilon)+\mathbf r_\epsilon(S), \qquad \|\mathbf r_\epsilon(S)\|_1\le C_r\epsilon, $$

where $C_r$ depends only on the displayed uniform bounds and the fixed coefficient bounds on $\mathcal K$, and is independent of $\epsilon$. Consequently,

$$ \sup_{0\le S\le S_*}\left(\|\mathbf X_\epsilon(S)-\mathbf X_N(S)\|_1+ \|\mathbf W_\epsilon(S)-\mathbf W_N(S)\|_1\right) \le C_r\epsilon S_*e^{L_fS_*}. $$

The estimate is conditional on existence and common compact containment through the specified finite scaled interval. It does not construct such a long-time family, solve Maxwell's equations for the prescribed fields, or produce a coupled Einstein–Maxwell family. In particular the $\sqrt\epsilon$ magnetic scaling can fail a coupled Einstein stress hierarchy unless additional matter scales are supplied.

Use the field, stress, matter, unit and curvature conventions of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and define the Einstein residual for the source-free field model by

$$ \mathscr R_{ab}(g,F;\Lambda):=G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}-\kappa T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}(g,F). $$

Suppose $G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=0$ on $U$, and let $F_0$ be a smooth real two-form with $dF_0=0$ and $d(\star_gF_0)=0$. For every real dimensionless $\delta$, the field $F_\delta:=\delta F_0$ obeys the same source-free Maxwell equations and

$$ \mathscr R_{ab}(g,F_\delta;\Lambda)=-\kappa\delta^2 T^{\mathrm{EM}}_{ab}(g,F_0). $$

This is an exact residual identity on the fixed metric. If $\delta\ne0$ and $F_0$ is nonzero at a point, its observer energy there is positive and the residual is nonzero there; this does not estimate the distance to a different coupled solution.

Separately, let $\rho,\sigma\in C^1(\Omega)$ and a $C^2$ future timelike field $U$ with $g(U,U)=-c^2$ define charged dust on an open $\Omega\subseteq U$, with $\rho>0$, $T_m^{ab}=\rho U^aU^b$, $j^a=\sigma U^a$, and the formal matter-exchange equation of [[def-emg-matter-formal-systems]]. For any dimensionless $\eta>0$, replacing $(\rho,\sigma)$ by $(\eta\rho,\eta\sigma)$ multiplies $T_m$ and $j$ by $\eta$, leaves $\alpha=\sigma/\rho$ unchanged, and leaves the dust acceleration equation $\rho U^a\nabla_aU^b=\sigma F^b{}_cU^c$ unchanged when the prescribed $F$ and $U$ are held fixed. The sourced Maxwell equation must still match the changed current. If both $F$ and $j$ are scaled by $\eta$, Maxwell's equations remain linear but the electromagnetic stress scales by $\eta^2$, whereas the dust stress scales by $\eta$; no general coupled-solution family follows.

For a flat background with $\Lambda=0$ and $T_m=0$, a nonzero source-free Maxwell field cannot solve the exact Einstein equation with the unchanged Minkowski metric, because its observer energy density is positive somewhere.

Finally, in Minkowski space consider only the prescribed Coulomb profile on the finite annulus $\mathcal A_\ell:=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:\ell<|\mathbf x|<2\ell\}$, where $\ell>0$ is a length, $Q\ne0$ is a charge, $r:=|\mathbf x|$, $\mathbf e_r:=\mathbf x/r$, $\mathbf E(\mathbf x)=Q(4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2)^{-1}\mathbf e_r$, and $\mathbf B=0$. Its Maxwell energy on that annulus is

$$ \mathcal E_\ell=\int_{\mathcal A_\ell}\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|\mathbf E|^2\,d^3x =\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0\ell}. $$

Thus this fixed-charge Coulomb cutoff family has diverging shell energy as $\ell\downarrow0$. This finite-annulus calculation asserts no point-source construction, self-field evaluation, or obstruction theorem for arbitrary regularizations.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

derivations.claim: In Minkowski coordinates $U=(\gamma c,\gamma\mathbf w)$, where $\gamma=(1-|\mathbf w|_2^2/c^2)^{-1/2}>0$.
